newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia presents regional plan to woo investors.
newsitem.headline: Serbia presents regional plan to woo investors.

text.p: Serbia presented an abridged version of its regional development plan until 2010 on Wednesday, expecting it to boost foreign investment by defining prospects and optimal conditions for the use of its territory.
"We expect the plan along with the earlier adopted law on concessions to attract foreign interest in big investment projects," the republic's Construction Minister Branislav Ivkovic said.
He said this was the first comprehensive document providing long-term guidelines on Serbia's regional development showing potential investors where and how much it was possible to invest.
"The plan proves that (investment) projects are rational, justified and profitable," Ivkovic said.
According to the law on management of natural resources by domestic and foreign companies, the government will grant concessions for exploration and exploitation of mineral ores.
The law, passed early in May, also envisages construction, maintainance and use of energy facilities, gas and oil pipelines, roads, railways, telecommunications, airports and other utilities.
"The law on concessions allows all those who invest here to cover their investment and make a profit," Ivkovic said.
But future investments had to help further development of the country and must be environmentally friendly, he added.
Foreign interest increased significantly since the laws on concessions and foreign investments were passed, he said.
The most interest was shown in a planned 700-million highway from Nis (south Serbia) to the Macedonian border and in investments in the power and oil industries and water-works.
The minister said concessions will be granted via international tenders.

Ile Kovacevic, director of the Yugoslav survey consulting firm, said foreign investors were already present in the country but were only doing market research and monitoring economic and legislative stability.
Since suspension of war-related U.N. sanctions in November 1995 until the end of June this year, 1,583 diverse foreign investment contracts were signed in Yugoslavia, Kovacevic said.
He gave no details of their value, but said they ranged from a few hundred thousand to one million German marks.

One Western analyst, who asked not to be named, said it was unlikely there would be any significant foreign capital inflow prior to country's full return to the international political and financial organisations. -- Belgrade Newsroom, 381 11 311 4254
